title: Virginia Resolves against the Stamp Act
summary: In March Parliament passed the Stamp Act, a tax on every newspaper, legal document and pack of cards in the colonies. In Virginia's House of Burgesses, the young lawyer Patrick Henry pushes through resolutions saying only Virginia's own assembly can tax Virginians.
significance: The resolves were printed across the colonies, often in a more radical form than the one passed, and gave the protest its slogan: no taxation without representation.

title: Stamp Act riots in Boston
summary: A crowd hangs an effigy of Andrew Oliver, the man appointed to sell the stamps, from an elm later called the Liberty Tree, then wrecks his office and house. He resigns the next day. Twelve days later a mob ransacks the mansion of Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson.
significance: Similar crowds forced stamp distributors to resign in nearly every colony, so the tax could never be collected. Groups calling themselves the Sons of Liberty grew out of the riots.

title: Stamp Act Congress
summary: Delegates from nine colonies meet in New York and send petitions to the King and Parliament. Merchants agree to stop buying British goods. In March 1766 Parliament repeals the Stamp Act, but declares it can still make laws for the colonies 'in all cases whatsoever'.
significance: The first time the colonies acted together against British policy. The repeal taught colonists that boycotts worked.

title: British troops land in Boston
summary: New duties on glass, paint, paper and tea, the Townshend Acts, bring new boycotts and attacks on customs officers. London sends two regiments of soldiers to keep order, and about 1,000 redcoats march into the town with drums beating.
significance: Soldiers camped on the Common and in public buildings of a town of about 15,000 people. Brawls between troops and townspeople became a daily event.

title: Boston Massacre
summary: A crowd throwing snowballs, ice and insults surrounds a sentry outside the Custom House. Captain Thomas Preston brings up a squad of soldiers, who fire into the crowd. Five men die, among them Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native descent.
significance: Paul Revere's engraving turned the brawl into propaganda. John Adams defended the soldiers in court and most were acquitted. The troops were withdrawn from the town.

title: Boston Tea Party
summary: The Tea Act lets the East India Company sell tea cheaply in America, with the old tax still included. Bostonians refuse to let three tea ships unload. At night, men loosely disguised as Mohawks board the ships and tip 342 chests of tea into the harbour.
significance: London decided Boston had to be punished, and the punishment united the other colonies behind Massachusetts.

title: Boston's port is closed
summary: Parliament's Coercive Acts, which colonists call the Intolerable Acts, close Boston's port until the tea is paid for, curb town meetings and put Massachusetts under General Thomas Gage as military governor. Other colonies send food and money to Boston.
significance: The acts turned a Boston quarrel into a crisis for all the colonies, which agreed to meet in Philadelphia.

title: First Continental Congress
summary: Fifty-six delegates from twelve colonies (Georgia stays away) meet for seven weeks. They agree a total boycott of British trade, set up local committees to enforce it, and petition the King. Most still hope for a settlement inside the empire.
significance: The committees became a rival government in every colony. Congress agreed to meet again in May 1775 if nothing changed.

title: 'Give me liberty, or give me death!'
summary: At a Virginia convention, Patrick Henry argues for raising a militia. His speech ends with the famous line, though the text we have was written down decades later by his biographer.
significance: Virginia, the largest colony, began arming. Its leaders, Washington and Jefferson among them, would shape the Revolution.
wiki: Give me liberty, or give me death!

title: Lexington: the first shots
summary: Gage sends about 700 soldiers at night to seize militia gunpowder and cannon at Concord. Paul Revere, William Dawes and others ride ahead to raise the alarm. At dawn about 77 militiamen stand on Lexington Green. Someone fires, nobody knows who, and the redcoats shoot down eight of them.
significance: The 'shot heard round the world'. Within hours, thousands of militia were marching on the British column.

title: Concord and the long retreat
stat: British: 73 killed. Colonists: 49 killed
summary: Militia drive British troops off Concord's North Bridge. On the 18-mile march back to Boston, militia fire from behind walls, trees and houses all along the road. Only a relief force sent from Boston saves the column.
significance: The British army had been beaten back by farmers. By the next morning about 15,000 militia had surrounded Boston.

title: The siege of Boston begins
summary: New England militia camp in a ring around Boston, from Roxbury to Cambridge and Charlestown Neck. Boston then stood on a near-island joined to the mainland by a narrow neck, so Gage's army is trapped there with the townspeople who stay.
significance: The siege lasted eleven months. The army gathered round Boston became the core of the Continental Army.

title: Capture of Fort Ticonderoga
summary: Ethan Allen's Green Mountain Boys and Benedict Arnold surprise the tiny British garrison of this fort on Lake Champlain at dawn and take it without a fight. The same day, the Second Continental Congress meets in Philadelphia.
significance: The fort held around 80 cannon. That winter they were dragged to Boston and used to drive the British out.

title: Washington chosen to command
summary: Congress adopts the army round Boston as the Continental Army and chooses George Washington, a Virginia planter who fought in the French and Indian War, as commander-in-chief. He takes command at Cambridge on 3 July.
significance: A Virginian in command of a New England army helped make the war a cause of all the colonies. Washington kept the job for the whole war, unpaid.
wiki: George Washington in the American Revolution

title: Battle of Bunker Hill
stat: British: 226 killed, 828 wounded. Americans: 115 killed
summary: Colonial troops fortify Breed's Hill overlooking Boston overnight. General William Howe attacks head-on. Two assaults are shot to pieces before the defenders run out of powder and the third takes the hill. Charlestown burns.
significance: A British victory that cost almost half the attacking force. Americans learned their militia could stand against regulars; Britain learned this would not be a short war.

title: Americans take Montreal
summary: Hoping Canada will join the rebellion as a fourteenth colony, Congress sends Richard Montgomery up Lake Champlain. After a long siege of Fort St. Jean he occupies Montreal without a fight. Meanwhile Benedict Arnold leads a starving column through the Maine wilderness toward Quebec City.
significance: The high point of the invasion of Canada. Most French Canadians stayed neutral, and few joined the Americans.

title: Dunmore's Proclamation
summary: Virginia's royal governor, Lord Dunmore, driven out of Williamsburg, promises freedom to enslaved people who leave Patriot masters and fight for the King. About 800 to 2,000 escape to his lines; many die of smallpox.
significance: It pushed many white Southern slaveholders into the rebellion. Over the war tens of thousands of enslaved people fled to the British, who offered freedom again in 1779.

title: Assault on Quebec City fails
stat: About 50 Americans killed and over 400 captured. British: under 20 casualties
summary: With enlistments running out at midnight, Montgomery and Arnold attack Quebec in a snowstorm. Montgomery is killed by grapeshot at the first barricade, Arnold is wounded, and Daniel Morgan's men are trapped in the narrow streets and captured.
significance: Canada stayed British. When British reinforcements arrived in May 1776 the Americans retreated, and by June they had left Montreal.

title: Common Sense
summary: Thomas Paine, an Englishman who had arrived in Philadelphia only 14 months before, publishes a pamphlet arguing in plain words that kings are absurd and that America should be independent. It sells perhaps 100,000 copies in a few months.
significance: Until then most colonists blamed the King's ministers, not the King. Paine made independence something ordinary people talked about.

title: The British leave Boston
summary: Henry Knox hauls the Ticonderoga cannon 300 miles on ox sleds over the winter. On the night of 4 March, Washington's men fortify Dorchester Heights, putting the guns over the town and harbour. Howe sails away to Halifax with his army and about 1,000 Loyalists.
significance: The first great American success. Boston stayed free of British troops for the rest of the war.

title: Charleston beats off the Royal Navy
summary: A British fleet bombards a half-built fort of palmetto logs and sand on Sullivan's Island. The soft logs absorb the cannonballs. The fort's guns badly damage the ships, and an attempt to land troops fails.
significance: Britain left the South alone for two and a half years. The palmetto tree is still on South Carolina's flag.

title: Declaration of Independence
summary: Congress votes for independence on 2 July and on 4 July approves the Declaration, drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson. It says that all men are created equal, with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and lists the King's crimes against the colonies.
significance: The rebels were now fighting for a new country. The promise of equality, made by men of whom many owned slaves, would be argued over for the next two centuries.

title: Battle of Long Island
stat: About 300 Americans killed and over 1,000 captured. British and Hessians: about 60 killed
summary: Howe lands the largest expedition Britain had ever sent overseas, about 32,000 soldiers including German troops hired from Hesse. His army marches round the American left flank at night and routs Washington's army. Two nights later Washington ferries his army across the East River to Manhattan in fog.
significance: The escape saved the army. Had Howe trapped it in Brooklyn, the war might have ended there.

title: The British take New York City
summary: British troops land at Kip's Bay after a heavy naval bombardment and the militia there run. Washington pulls his army north to Harlem Heights. Days later a great fire destroys about a quarter of the city.
significance: New York became Britain's main base for the rest of the war and a haven for Loyalists. It was the last city the British gave up, in November 1783.

title: Battle of Valcour Island
summary: Benedict Arnold's makeshift fleet of gunboats, built that summer, fights a much stronger British squadron on Lake Champlain. Most of his boats are destroyed over two days.
significance: A defeat that won time. With winter coming, the British gave up their advance on Ticonderoga until the following year.

title: Fall of Fort Washington
stat: About 2,800 Americans captured. British and Hessians: 84 killed
summary: The last American stronghold on Manhattan falls to an assault by Hessian and British troops. Almost the whole garrison is captured, and many of them later die in the prison ships moored off Brooklyn.
significance: Washington retreated across New Jersey with a shrinking army. Many thought the rebellion was finished.

title: Washington crosses the Delaware
summary: On Christmas night about 2,400 men cross the ice-choked Delaware River in boats in a sleet storm, with horses and 18 cannon. Two other crossings planned for the same night fail.
significance: Thomas Paine had just written: 'These are the times that try men's souls.' Washington needed a victory before most of his soldiers' enlistments ran out on 31 December.
wiki: Washington's crossing of the Delaware River

title: Battle of Trenton
stat: Hessians: 22 killed, about 900 captured. Americans: none killed in the fighting
summary: After a nine-mile night march in the storm, Washington's men attack the Hessian garrison of Trenton at about eight in the morning. In under an hour the Hessians are surrounded and surrender. Their commander, Colonel Rall, is mortally wounded.
significance: A small battle with a huge effect. Men re-enlisted, recruits came in, and the rebellion survived the winter.

title: Battle of Princeton
summary: Leaving his campfires burning to fool Cornwallis's army at Trenton, Washington slips round it at night and beats the British rearguard at Princeton. General Hugh Mercer is bayoneted and dies of his wounds; Washington rides in to rally the line himself.
significance: The British pulled back from most of New Jersey. Washington's army spent the winter safe in the hills at Morristown.

title: Battle of Bennington
summary: General John Burgoyne's army has come south from Canada and retaken Fort Ticonderoga in July. He sends about 800 German troops, Loyalists and Native warriors to seize horses and supplies at Bennington. New England militia under John Stark surround and destroy them, and then a relief column.
significance: Burgoyne lost almost a tenth of his army and the supplies he needed. Militia now poured in to oppose him.

title: Battle of Brandywine
stat: Roughly 1,300 American and 590 British casualties
summary: Howe sails his army from New York to the head of Chesapeake Bay and marches on Philadelphia. At Brandywine Creek he repeats the Long Island plan: a column marches round Washington's right flank and the Americans are driven back. The young Marquis de Lafayette is wounded in his first battle.
significance: On 26 September British troops marched into Philadelphia, the American capital. Congress fled to York, Pennsylvania.

title: Saratoga: Freeman's Farm
stat: British: about 600 casualties. Americans: about 300
summary: Burgoyne tries to push past the American army entrenched on Bemis Heights, blocking the road to Albany. In a day of fighting around a clearing, Daniel Morgan's riflemen pick off British officers. The British hold the field but lose twice as many men.
significance: Burgoyne dug in and waited for help from New York that never came, while the American army grew every day.

title: Battle of Germantown
stat: Americans: about 1,100 casualties, including over 400 captured. British: about 530
summary: Washington attacks the main British camp at Germantown with four columns at dawn. Fog, a stone house held by British troops, and American columns firing on each other turn an early success into a retreat.
significance: Another defeat, but a near thing. It helped persuade France that the Americans could fight.

title: Saratoga: Bemis Heights
stat: British: several hundred killed, wounded or captured. Americans: about 150
summary: Burgoyne probes the American lines with about 1,500 men. Horatio Gates's army counter-attacks. Benedict Arnold, without a command after quarrelling with Gates, rides into the fight and leads the storming of a German redoubt before he is shot in the leg.
significance: Burgoyne retreated to Saratoga and was surrounded there by an army three times the size of his own.

title: Burgoyne surrenders at Saratoga
stat: About 6,000 British and German soldiers surrender
summary: Out of food and surrounded, Burgoyne's whole army lays down its arms. Under the terms, called a 'convention', the men were to be shipped home, but Congress went back on the deal and held them prisoner for the rest of the war.
significance: The turning point. A whole British army had been captured, and France now believed the Americans could win.

title: Winter at Valley Forge
stat: Perhaps 1,700 to 2,000 soldiers died of disease
summary: About 12,000 soldiers march into winter camp 18 miles from Philadelphia and build log huts. Food, clothing and blankets run short, and typhus, typhoid and dysentery kill many. From February, Baron von Steuben, a Prussian officer, drills the army in a single system.
significance: The army that marched out in June was smaller but far better trained, and it held together under Washington.

title: Alliance with France
summary: Benjamin Franklin and two other American envoys sign treaties of trade and alliance with France. France had been sending money and guns in secret since 1776; now it recognises the United States and goes to war with Britain.
significance: The war became a world war. Britain had to defend the Caribbean, India and Britain itself, and the French navy could now challenge British control of the sea.

title: Battle of Monmouth
stat: About 360 American and 360 to 1,100 British casualties (estimates vary). Dozens on both sides died of heat
summary: With a French fleet on its way, the new British commander, Sir Henry Clinton, abandons Philadelphia and marches for New York. Washington attacks his rearguard on a day near 100°F. Charles Lee's advance guard falls back in confusion until Washington arrives to steady the army.
significance: A draw, but the army trained at Valley Forge stood up to British regulars in open battle. It was the last big battle in the north.

title: Cherry Valley raid
stat: About 30 civilians and 16 soldiers killed
summary: Loyalist rangers under Walter Butler and Seneca and Mohawk warriors under Joseph Brant attack a frontier settlement and its fort. Many of the dead are women and children. The raiders were partly avenging the burning of the Iroquois towns of Unadilla and Onaquaga by Patriot troops that autumn.
significance: The New York frontier became a war of raids and reprisals. Congress answered with a campaign to destroy the Iroquois towns.

title: Britain takes Savannah
summary: Britain switches its effort south, expecting thousands of Loyalists to rise. About 3,000 troops from New York land below Savannah and, guided along a hidden path through a swamp, rout the defenders.
significance: Georgia's royal governor returned, and Georgia became the only colony where royal government was restored during the war.

title: George Rogers Clark takes Vincennes
summary: In 1778 a small Virginian force under Clark took the French villages of the Illinois country. When the British governor of Detroit, Henry Hamilton, retakes Vincennes, Clark marches about 170 men through 180 miles of flooded prairie in February and forces him to surrender.
significance: Virginia's hold on the Illinois country later helped American negotiators claim the land to the Mississippi in 1783.

title: The Sullivan expedition
summary: On Washington's orders, about 4,000 Continental soldiers under John Sullivan march into Iroquois country. They defeat a Loyalist and Iroquois force at Newtown, then burn over 40 Seneca and Cayuga towns, their orchards and their stores of corn.
significance: Thousands of Iroquois fled to Fort Niagara and many died there that winter. The raids on the frontier did not stop; they grew fiercer.

title: Spain takes Baton Rouge
summary: Spain declares war on Britain in June 1779, as France's ally rather than America's. Bernardo de Gálvez, governor of Spanish Louisiana, strikes first: he takes the British forts on the lower Mississippi, then Baton Rouge, whose surrender also hands over Natchez.
significance: Gálvez went on to take Mobile in 1780 and Pensacola in 1781, removing Britain from the Gulf coast.

title: French and Americans fail at Savannah
stat: French and Americans: about 244 killed. British: about 40
summary: Admiral d'Estaing's French fleet and army join Benjamin Lincoln's Americans to retake Savannah. After a short siege they storm the British lines at dawn and are cut down. The Polish cavalry officer Casimir Pulaski is mortally wounded.
significance: The bloodiest hour of the war for the allies. The French sailed away, and the British were free to attack Charleston.

title: Fall of Charleston
stat: About 5,000 Americans taken prisoner
summary: Clinton sails from New York with about 8,500 troops, lands south of Charleston and lays siege to the city, trapping Lincoln's army on its peninsula. After six weeks and a heavy bombardment, Lincoln surrenders.
significance: The worst American defeat of the war. The whole southern army was gone, and Britain set up posts across South Carolina.

title: The Waxhaws
stat: Americans: 113 killed. British: 5 killed
summary: Banastre Tarleton's British Legion, Loyalist cavalry and infantry, catches a retreating Virginian regiment under Abraham Buford near the North Carolina border. Many Americans are killed after trying to surrender.
significance: 'Tarleton's quarter' came to mean no mercy, and the story drove many backcountry men to join the Patriot militia.

title: Battle of Camden
stat: About 1,900 Americans killed, wounded or captured. British: about 320 casualties
summary: Horatio Gates, the victor of Saratoga, leads a new southern army against Cornwallis. His Virginia and North Carolina militia break at the first British bayonet charge. Baron de Kalb's Continentals fight on until they are overwhelmed and de Kalb is killed. Gates rides 60 miles from the field.
significance: Another southern army destroyed. Congress replaced Gates with Washington's choice, Nathanael Greene.

title: Benedict Arnold's treason
summary: Arnold, the hero of Quebec and Saratoga, now commanding the fortress at West Point, has been secretly selling plans to hand it to the British. Their go-between, Major John André, is caught near Tarrytown on 23 September with the plans in his boot. Arnold escapes to a British warship.
significance: West Point guarded the Hudson, the link between New England and the other states. André was hanged as a spy; Arnold became a British general.

title: Battle of Kings Mountain
stat: Loyalists: about 290 killed and 660 captured. Patriots: 28 killed
summary: Major Patrick Ferguson leads about 1,000 Loyalist militia. Frontier militia from over the mountains, the 'Overmountain Men', surround his camp on a wooded ridge and climb it from all sides, firing from behind trees. Ferguson is shot from his horse. Almost all of the battle was fought between Americans.
significance: Cornwallis abandoned his first invasion of North Carolina. Thomas Jefferson called it the turn of the tide in the south.

title: Battle of Cowpens
stat: British: about 110 killed and about 700 captured. Americans: about 25 killed
summary: Greene splits his small army. Daniel Morgan's detachment, chased by Tarleton, turns to fight in an open pasture. Morgan puts his militia in front and asks them for just two volleys before falling back, with his Continentals on a rise behind. Tarleton's men charge, think the Americans are running, and are caught in a double envelopment.
significance: Tarleton's force was almost wiped out in under an hour. Cornwallis burned his own baggage to chase Greene across North Carolina, wearing out his army.

title: Battle of Guilford Courthouse
stat: British: 93 killed and over 400 wounded, a quarter of the army. Americans: 79 killed
summary: After the 'race to the Dan', Greene turns to fight with three lines, copying Cowpens. Cornwallis's 1,900 men break through all three, but Greene withdraws his army in good order. Cornwallis fires grapeshot into the mêlée to stop the Americans, hitting his own men too.
significance: A British victory that crippled the British army. Cornwallis left the Carolinas for the coast, then marched into Virginia.

title: Spain takes Pensacola
summary: Gálvez sails his ships into Pensacola Bay under fire after his senior naval officer refuses to. After a two-month siege by Spanish and French troops, a Spanish shell blows up the main British powder magazine, and the garrison of over 1,100 surrenders.
significance: West Florida became Spanish. Britain had now lost the Gulf of Mexico as well as the Mississippi.

title: The march to Virginia
place: Dobbs Ferry and Philipsburg, New York
summary: Word arrives that Admiral de Grasse is bringing the French West Indies fleet to Chesapeake Bay. Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau drop their plan to attack New York and march about 7,000 American and French soldiers 450 miles south, while fake camps and bread ovens in New Jersey make Clinton think New York is still the target.
significance: The only time in the war that land and sea forces of the allies came together at exactly the right place.

title: Battle of the Chesapeake
summary: A British fleet under Admiral Graves arrives from New York and finds de Grasse's larger fleet already in the bay. They fight for about two hours off the capes. Neither side loses a ship, but after days of manoeuvring Graves goes back to New York for repairs.
significance: Perhaps the most important sea battle of the century. With the French holding the bay, Cornwallis could not be rescued or escape by sea.

title: Cornwallis surrenders at Yorktown
stat: About 8,000 British and German soldiers and sailors surrender
summary: About 16,000 American and French soldiers lay siege to Cornwallis's fortified base. French guns batter the town, and on 14 October two key redoubts are stormed at night, one by Americans under Alexander Hamilton and one by the French. Cornwallis surrenders; his men march out between lines of French and Americans.
significance: When the news reached London, Prime Minister Lord North reportedly cried 'Oh God, it is all over.' Parliament voted to end the war in America.

title: Gnadenhutten massacre
summary: Pennsylvania militia hunting raiders seize a village of Christian Lenape (Delaware) who had stayed neutral. Accusing them of the raids, they kill 28 men, 29 women and 39 children with mallets and hatchets, then burn the village.
significance: On the frontier the war went on after Yorktown, and grew more savage. The Lenape and their allies took revenge that summer.

title: Washington stops the Newburgh conspiracy
place: New Windsor Cantonment, near Newburgh, New York
summary: Unpaid for months and fearing they will be sent home with nothing, army officers circulate an anonymous call to defy Congress. Washington surprises their meeting. Putting on his glasses to read a letter, he says he has grown grey in their service and now finds himself growing blind.
significance: The officers backed down. The army stayed under civilian control, a choice that shaped the new republic.

title: Treaty of Paris
summary: Franklin, John Adams and John Jay sign a peace with Britain. Britain recognises the independence of the United States, with borders running west to the Mississippi. The same day Britain makes peace with France and Spain, and gives Florida back to Spain.
significance: The new country was twice the size of the thirteen colonies. The Indigenous nations who lived west of the mountains, many of them Britain's allies, were not consulted, and their land was signed away.

title: The British leave New York
summary: The last British troops sail from New York, seven years after they took it. Washington's army marches in. Some 29,000 Loyalists had already left New York for Nova Scotia, Britain or the Caribbean, and with them about 3,000 Black Loyalists who had won their freedom.
significance: New Yorkers celebrated 'Evacuation Day' every 25 November for more than a century.

title: Washington resigns his commission
summary: Congress is meeting in Annapolis. Washington hands back his commission as commander-in-chief and goes home to Mount Vernon in time for Christmas.
significance: Victorious generals rarely gave up power. When King George III heard Washington would do it, he is said to have called him the greatest man in the world.
